speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: If Mr Yip is satisfied with the response, he may wish to withdraw his question after this session.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Assoc Prof Jamus Lim asked about the components of the net loss, including from the Monetary Authority of Singapore's (MAS) currency intervention.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: MAS had explained in detail the constituents of its reported financial loss at its annual press conference in July, which I will reiterate here.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The negative currency translation effects arise because the Official Foreign Reserves (OFR) are held in foreign currencies but reported in Singapore dollars.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Therefore, a stronger Singapore dollar will result in a lower value for the OFR when expressed in Singapore dollar terms.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: This currency translation effect does not have any bearing on the external purchasing power of the OFR or on MAS' ability to conduct monetary policy.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The net interest expense incurred on MAS' money market operations to mop up this excess liquidity in the banking system was unusually large in the last FY due to two factors: one, the large volume of operations; and two, higher interest rates.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The high volume of money market operations was necessitated by MAS' interventions in the foreign exchange market to moderate the appreciation of the Singapore dollar.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: As MAS explained earlier, had it not done this, the Singapore dollar would have been too strong and therefore hurt the economy.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: While this currency intervention added substantially to our OFR, it created excess Singapore dollar liquidity in our domestic banking system which MAS had to remove and, therefore, incur an interest expense in the process.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Mr Don Wee asked if MAS plans to increase the interest yields and payments of Treasury Bills and bonds to curb losses and encourage a higher level of savings.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Such instruments are issued by the Government and not by MAS.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The interest rates payable on such instruments are not determined by MAS but are market-determined via auctions.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: As the interest rates of such instruments have increased in tandem with the rise in global interest rates, we have already seen a healthy pick-up in demand by the public.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng asked whether there are plans to broaden the basket of currencies in which the OFR is held.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The OFR is already held in a diverse range of currencies.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: As long as the Singapore dollar appreciates against these currencies, there will be negative currency translation effects.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: In the last FY, the Singapore dollar appreciated against every major currency.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: As MAS explained earlier, the effects of a stronger Singapore dollar cannot be hedged or diversified away.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Ms Hazel Poa asked about the benefits of a stronger Singapore dollar in view of the financial losses recorded by MAS.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The appreciation of the Singapore dollar last year reflected the outcome of MAS' tighter monetary policy to dampen inflation.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: This policy has been successful in curbing imported inflationary pressures.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Between May 2022 and June 2023, Singapore's import price index had fallen by some 14%.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: This decline in import prices has, in turn, contributed to lower domestic inflation.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng asked how MAS strikes a balance between managing inflation and incurring losses and whether these losses are anticipated.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: MAS' monetary policy is focused purely on keeping inflation low and ensuring medium-term price stability.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: It does not take into account any potential impact on MAS' profits because to do so would undermine its mission.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: This is similar to how other major central banks conduct monetary policy.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Many of them have also reported losses arising from their monetary policy operations.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: MAS' financial performance is a necessary consequence of its conduct of monetary policy.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The OFR is key in enabling MAS to conduct effective monetary policy.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: As a central bank, MAS adopts a conservative approach in its investments, with a significant proportion of its portfolio invested in liquid financial market instruments.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Through a well-diversified portfolio and careful risk management, MAS expects to earn good long-term returns that are commensurate with its risk profile.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: MAS contributes to the Government's budget in two ways.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: First, under the Net Investment Returns (NIR) framework, the Government can spend up to 50% of the expected long-term real return on the assets invested by MAS, GIC and Temasek.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: NIR is based on the long-term expected returns of these entities and, hence, is not affected by their short-term performance.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Accordingly, MAS' reported net loss in the last FY has no impact on the NIR that is available to the Government.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Second, similar to other Statutory Boards, MAS makes contributions to the Government's Consolidated Fund in lieu of corporate income tax.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: This is based on 17% of the net profit for the year, after offsetting cumulative losses from previous financial years.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The Government recognises that MAS contributions will vary considerably from year to year and has therefore smoothened the revenue volatility by requiring the annual contributions made by MAS to be paid in equal proportions over a period of three years.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Given the net loss in FY2022/2023, MAS will not accrue a contribution to the Government's Consolidated Fund for that financial year.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: In sum, MAS’ overarching mandate is to ensure macroeconomic stability.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: MAS’ monetary policy has helped to deliver broad macroeconomic stability for over 40 years as the basis for sustained economic growth and increases in real incomes for Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Minister of State has said that the benefit of the strong dollar policy is to dampen inflation.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Given that domestic consumption is $192 billion and this recorded loss of $30.8 billion is a big sum of money, equivalent to about 16% of domestic consumption, how much has it dampened inflation and compared to the $30.8 billion, what is the official cost-benefit analysis and the assessment on the efficacy of this policy?

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: As I mentioned earlier in my reply, the loss is attributed to 70% in net currency translation losses and a 30% in interventions and money market operations.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: These are the normal functionings of how central banks conduct monetary policy and with its goal to dampen inflation and to have medium-term price stability – so that is to put that into context.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: So, inflation would have stayed higher for much longer and brought about much more significant increases in the cost of living for households.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Therefore, MAS' conduct of monetary policy has made an impact.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: We are still seeing the impact over the course of the different quarters, having tightened monetary policy five times since October 2021.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: One motivation behind my request for a breakdown in the numbers was because MAS had previously explained that it would strategically strengthen the Singapore dollar for the purposes of addressing imported inflation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This was a move that I supported, and, in fact, Minister of State Tan has reiterated this MAS position that the Singapore dollar has, indeed, appreciated against every major currency.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: That said, based on my understanding of the data, between January and July 2023, the movements of the Singapore dollar were essentially the converse of the US dollar.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In particular, when there is a strengthening of the US dollar, the Singapore dollar would weaken and when the US dollar weakened, the Singapore dollar would strengthen.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In particular, for the US dollar's two most recent peaks at the beginning of June and July, this broadly corresponded to troughs in the Singapore dollar-US dollar rates.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This actually suggests to me that MAS was not really leaning that much against the wind; or if it did, it was not doing so with sufficient interventions that would have altered the overall US dollar trends.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And, therefore, attributing losses, the 30% that the Minister of State Tan mentioned, to sufficient interventions does not strike me as credible.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: So, my follow-up question then is whether the MAS actually views this earlier strong dollar policy as successful and, if so, why in March it announced a decision to ease the Singapore dollar policy?

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: I think it is really important to note that the Singapore dollar is trade-weighted against a basket of currencies, not just the US dollar.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Therefore, you need to look at it as a whole basket of currencies.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: We look at it from very much over the long term.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: First, on currency translation effects, I have explained that technically.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The second is on currency intervention and as well as money market operations.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Had it not done so, then you could worsen inflation.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: But when you sell Singapore dollars into the domestic banking system, you will then have to undertake money market operations.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: This is the normal conduct of central banking policy.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: What the MAS then does is to sell repurchase agreements (repos) or MAS bills, of which it then has to pay interest payments on.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: And these interests, in line with global interest rates, have risen.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: And, therefore, when we issue an MAS bill, for example, we would have to pay a higher interest rate.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: That adds to that 30% account of the loss that we are talking about today.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: So, just explaining the technicalities of how this works; trade-weighted as well as why we need to conduct money market operations to moderate the appreciation of the Singapore dollar.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Can I confirm with the Minister of State the loss is a result of currency translation as well as money market operations, so as to help Singaporeans, especially the SMEs to cope with the rising business costs as well as the rising cost of living?

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: In fact, that is the whole purpose of MAS' monetary policy – it is to manage price stability as well as to manage inflation, and we have done so.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: I explained in my reply to Parliamentary Questions and the supplementary question by Ms Hazel Poa.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Had we not done so, I think the cost of living would be higher, imported inflation would be also higher.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I wish to ask how have MAS' investments been thus far and its impact on our official foreign reserves.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: MAS made a small gain of $0.6 billion on its investment portfolio amidst a depressed market environment.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: And last year, as Members would know, was an unusual year for financial markets, where bond markets and equity markets performed very badly.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: In this case, MAS' investment performance had to be viewed from a longer-term perspective.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Since the 2008 Global Financial Crisis, MAS' investment portfolio had benefited from an unusual period of low inflation as well as low interest rates.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Notwithstanding the financial loss that we had been discussing, MAS' OFR position remains strong and it re-transferred S$191 billion of excess OFR to the Government.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: If I may just quickly clarify my earlier supplementary question?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: I appreciate what Minister of State Tan shared about how the Singapore dollar is measured against a basket of currencies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: But, in particular, could I confirm with him that MAS did, indeed, reverse its strong dollar policy in March of this year?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: And, if so, what were the factors that led to its decision to subsequently make that reversal after making a case for strengthening the Singapore dollar?

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: As I mentioned to the Member earlier on, it is measured against a trade-weighted basket of currencies.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: We have tightened monetary policy five times since 2021, and there was no such announcement.
